paper_sections.title: Individual Differences in Anticipatory Somatosensory Cortex Activity for Shock is Positively Related with Trait Anxiety and Multisensory Integration
2.6. General Region of Interest Analysis and Correlation
3.3. Primary Somatosensory Cortex and Individual Differences Analyses

description.value: The study examined whether anticipatory somatosensory activity during fear conditioning varied with trait anxiety and whether activity in auditory and amygdala regions related to activity in primary somatosensory cortex.

design.value: A within-participant fear-conditioning fMRI study with 30 randomly ordered trials: 10 CS+ trials with shock, 10 non-reinforced CS+ trials, and 10 CS− trials. The tone assigned as CS+ was counterbalanced across participants, and the main analyses focused on the tone interval before the possible shock.

name.value: standard Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) 2 mm brain

description.value: An established measure of individual differences in anxiety, with state anxiety (STAI-S) and trait anxiety (STAI-T) scores completed before the fMRI scan.

assessment_type.value: measure of individual differences in anxiety

description.value: Fear contingent responding was assessed using peak skin conductance response amplitude from baseline, extracted 1–8 s after tone onset and averaged as a function of CS tone.

name.value: non-reinforced CS+ trials and CS− trials

source_definition.value: The first two critical regressors were for non-reinforced CS+ trials and CS− trials.
Shock-reinforced trials were modeled as covariates of no interest.
Six motion parameters were modeled as covariates of no interest.
Individual trait anxiety measured by the STAI-T score.

name.value: global mean signal level over all brain voxels

source_definition.value: The global mean signal level over all brain voxels was included to reduce the confounding effects of the global signal change.
Activity in the right S1 region corresponding to shock delivery to the left hand.
Activity in the left S1 region, described as the non-shock-related region associated with the right hand.
Activity in bilateral auditory regions, identified as A1 regions corresponding to the initial sensory input from the tones.
Activity in the bilateral amygdala anatomical ROI.

description.value: Twenty healthy participants (11 female) with mean age of 21.95 (range 18–35) participated in the study.

excluded_count.value: no participants were excluded from the analysis post hoc due to issues of data quality

inclusion_criteria.value: Safe for participation in the MRI environment

exclusion_criteria.value: Participants who self-reported having a clinically diagnosed mental illness
Participants who reported being on, or having taken in the past, any pharmacological intervention for a mental illness

medication_status.value: No participants reported being on, or having taken in the past, any pharmacological intervention for a mental illness.

task_description.value: Two tones, 500 and 1500 Hz, were used as conditioned stimuli. One tone was paired with a mild electric shock to the third and fourth fingers of the left hand. The task consisted of 30 trials presented in random order: 10 CS+ with shock, 10 CS+ without shock, and 10 CS− tones. CS+ tones were followed by shock with a 50% partial reinforcement schedule. Trials that included shocks were excluded in subsequent analyses.

presentation_software.value: PsychToolbox extensions based on Matlab 2010b (MathWorks Corp., Natrick, MA, USA)

instructions.value: Participants were asked to indicate by button press with their index or middle finger of the right hand whether the tone was low or high pitched immediately after hearing the tone. Participants were informed of which CS would be paired with shock prior to study commencement.

stimuli.value: Two tones (500 and 1500 Hz) adopted as conditioned stimuli; a mild electric shock used as an unconditioned stimulus.

task_performance_measures.value: Button-press discrimination of whether the tone was low or high pitched

task_name.value: separate task following the conditioning phase

task_description.value: The imaging session also involved a separate task following the conditioning phase; the details of this independent task were described previously by Lee et al. (2014).

instrument.value: Siemens 3T Magnetom Trio with a 32-channel matrix head coil

description.value: High-resolution T1-MPRAGE structural images were acquired first with repetition time (TR) = 1950 ms, echo time (TE) = 2.26 ms, flip angle (FA) = 7°, 1 mm isotropic voxel, and 256 mm field of view.

modality.value: functional images with gradient-echo echo-planar T2*-weighted imaging

instrument.value: Siemens 3T Magnetom Trio with a 32-channel matrix head coil

description.value: Each functional volume consisted of 40 interleaved (no skip) 2.5 mm axial T2*-weighted slices; TR = 2000 ms; TE = 25 ms; FA = 90°; matrix size = 64 × 64; field of view = 192 mm.

instrument.value: MP-150 system (BIOPAC System, Goleta, CA, USA)

description.value: Individual skin conductance responses were acquired with MRI-compatible electrodes placed on the index and middle finger of the left hand. All physiological data were recorded at 1 kHz through the MP-150 system, connected to a grounded RF filter and MR-compatible leads and electrodes.

reason_no_modality_class_used.value: Skin conductance is a physiological recording and is not covered by the MRI, EEG, fNIRS, or PET classes.

description.value: Standard preprocessing was conducted using FMRIBs Software Library (FSL), including slice-time correction, motion correction, spatial smoothing, high-pass temporal filtering, skull stripping of structural images, registration of each functional image to the participant’s high-resolution structural image and the standard MNI 2 mm brain, and removal of noise components with MELODIC ICA2. The first eight volumes were discarded to allow for signal equilibration.

steps.value: The first eight volumes were discarded to allow for signal equilibration.
Spatial smoothing with a Gaussian kernel of full width at half maximum (FWHM) 6 mm
High-pass temporal filtering with a filter width of 100 s
Skull stripping of structural images with FSL’s Brain Extraction Tool (BET)
Registering each functional image to both the participant’s high-resolution structural image and the standard Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) 2 mm brain
MELODIC ICA2 was applied to remove noise components.

model_settings.value: BOLD signal was estimated during the CS tone interval using regressors for non-reinforced CS+ trials and CS− trials. Six motion parameters and shock-reinforced trials were modeled as covariates of no interest.

model_type.value: whole-brain group-level random-effects general linear model

model_settings.value: The whole-brain group-level analysis was thresholded using cluster detection statistics, with a height threshold of Z > 2.3 and cluster corrected to p < 0.05, one-tailed. Whole-brain multiple comparisons correction was carried out using Gaussian Random Field Theory.

hrf_model.value: same temporal epoch for both non-reinforced CS+ and CS− trials

model_settings.value: The shock epoch on reinforced CS+ trials was modeled for 500 ms, using the same temporal epoch for both non-reinforced CS+ and CS− trials. Results were analyzed using anatomical ROIs of right and left S1.

A new design matrix contained unique trial-by-trial regressors for CS+ no shock and CS− trials, resulting in 20 independent variables. Global mean signal, motion parameters, and shock trials were included as covariates of no interest. Mean parameter estimates from the S1 seed were correlated with signal from all other brain voxels, and correlation magnitudes were converted into z scores using the Fisher’s r-to-z transformation.

Initial individual differences analyses between STAI-T, S1, A1, and amygdala activity were carried out using the robust correlation method, which identifies bivariate outliers and removes them in the calculation of a 95% confidence interval.

estimator.value: robust Pearson correlation with bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals

model_settings.value: The mediation analysis evaluated the total effect c, indirect path a, indirect path b, direct effect c′ after controlling for the indirect path, and mediation effect ab, using mean responses in each region per participant and signal differences between CS+ and CS−.

model_representation_notes.value: A new design matrix was created where unique trial-by-trial regressors were created for each condition of interest, resulting in 20 independent variables (10 CS+ tones and 10 CS− tones).

interpretations.value: Increased connectivity during CS+ trials between right S1 and bilateral dlPFC and dmPFC.

model_representation_notes.value: A new design matrix was created where unique trial-by-trial regressors were created for each condition of interest, resulting in 20 independent variables (10 CS+ tones and 10 CS− tones).

interpretations.value: Decreased connectivity during CS+ trials between right S1 and parts of lingual gyrus.

model_representation_notes.value: The regressors were modeled using a gamma-variate function plus temporal derivative; six motion parameters and shock-reinforced trials were modeled as covariates of no interest.

interpretations.value: Greater activity for CS+ compared to CS− trials in the putative fear network, including insula, dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, and thalamus; a similar pattern of activity in auditory cortices, and a larger cluster that included parts of the right motor and somatosensory cortices.
